question: Children’s online safety – from bans to proactive protection

Children’s online safety is a growing concern. EU policy remains reliant on risk frameworks, access rules, bans and other control mechanisms. There is evidence to suggest that restrictions, bans and monitoring are ineffective or even counterproductive1.

Applying the same restrictions to very different technologies and to children of different ages and in different stages of development can weaken trust, limit children’s rights and agency, and push digital consumption into other online spaces.

An evidence-based approach would 1) use scientific instruments to assess and improve design options, 2) anticipate risks and treat children’s safety as a proactive design challenge and 3) establish preventative guardrails that protect children while also supporting their rights, agency and well-being. 1.
Is the Commission, jointly with the Member States, considering a proactive and systematic approach, recognising children as active participants?
Is the Commission considering aligning its policy with evidence that supports the promotion of rights, safety and privacy by design, as reflected in international legal instruments?
Is the Commission considering increasing support for disciplinary and interdisciplinary research to close gaps in understanding the interplay between risks, opportunities and digital environments?
Cortesi, S., & Gasser, U. (2026). Digital child safety at the frontier: From evidence to action. Science (New York, N.Y.), 392(6793), 30-32. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7804.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The Commission is strengthening interdisciplinary evidence gathering. A Special Panel was established with a mandate to draw up recommendations to the President of the Commission on child safety online and potential age restrictions1. It brings together youth representatives and experts from health, neuroscience, technology and the child rights field.

The panel has held two meetings thus far, assessing the evidence of risks and opportunities for minors in digital environments and how to strengthen existing rules. Building upon the EU’s toolbox for protecting minors online, and based on the independent, evidence-based input from experts, the co-chairs of the panel will submit their recommendations by July 2026.

Moreover, the EU has already in place comprehensive framework for protecting, and empowering minors online. In particular, the Digital Services Act (DSA)2 requires the providers of all platforms accessible to minors to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security.
The guidelines on the protection of minors3 under the DSA are based on the principle of respecting children’s rights, privacy, safety, and security by design.

Complementing these efforts, the Better Internet for Kids strategy supports safer and more age-appropriate digital environments with the involvement of children in policymaking as one of its core pillars, including through initiatives such as the Youth Ambassadors programme. The upcoming Digital Fairness Act4 aims to strengthen consumer protection online with a particular focus on minors.
